problem_shape: This family is about systems that need facts to be connected, not just stored. A knowledge graph is a map of things and relations: a person works for an organization, a chemical has a property, a product belongs to a category, a medical answer follows a disease relation, or an event changes another event. The shared real-world problem is that many tasks need this connected map to answer questions, recommend items, detect fraud, verify claims, monitor contaminants, or explain a model decision. A single document, image, table, or transaction often gives only a fragment. The useful evidence sits in paths, neighborhoods, relation types, time changes, and missing links. The input evidence shows 123 papers across WWW, SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD using graphs for question answering, recommendation, fraud detection, scientific extraction, dynamic crawling, fact checking, table search, scene reasoning, and graph generation. They belong together because each paper asks how to turn scattered facts into a structure where evidence can be followed, checked, completed, updated, or protected.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would first make a simple fact table or a simple set of links, then search it directly. For a question, fetch the nearest facts. For recommendation, connect users to liked items. For extraction, ask a language model to list entities and properties. For completion, predict the missing edge that looks most similar to known edges. This breaks because knowledge graphs are incomplete, noisy, and uneven. A shortest path may be cheap but miss the meaning of the relation. A language model may write a fluent property that is inconsistent with the graph. A graph for medicine or fact checking can be dangerous when a missing or poisoned subgraph looks authoritative. Multimodal graphs add another failure: text, images, and structure may disagree. Dynamic graphs add time, so yesterday's map may forget new facts or overwrite old ones.
mathematical_principle: The central mathematical idea is structured evidence movement. The system first decides what counts as an object, what counts as a relation, and what information is allowed to travel across a relation. Then it scores possible paths, neighbors, missing links, extracted properties, or candidate answers by asking whether they fit both the local facts and the wider map. In plain language, a relation is not just a line; it is a claim about how two things should constrain each other. If a drug treats a disease, nearby medical facts can support an answer, but only if the path follows medically meaningful steps. If a user likes an item, item-side facts can help recommendation, but user-side scarcity and noisy links must be handled. If a claim has sub-claims, the graph can schedule which dependency to verify first. Some papers compare paths, some estimate confidence, some generate plausible missing structure, some mine rules, and some compress or profile the graph. The tradeoff is link-following versus link-skepticism: use the map enough to combine evidence, but not so much that wrong, missing, stale, or attacker-made links control the answer.
why_math_matters: The math matters because connected facts create more possibilities than a person can safely handle by rules. A question over a large graph may have many possible paths; S-Path-RAG treats path choice as a measured search so the answer system does not spend words on irrelevant routes. HyperRAG changes the shape of the map when a fact involves more than two things, because splitting one complex fact into pairs can make reasoning drift. Calibration work asks when an answer should be less confident because the retrieved subgraph is incomplete or unreliable. Rule mining such as MiniAMIE needs shortcuts because checking every possible rule in a large graph costs too much time. Multimodal papers need scoring because images, text, and relation structure are useful in different amounts for different relations. The world structure being exploited is that facts constrain one another: related objects make some answers more believable and others less believable. The same structure can mislead when links are copied, stale, sparse, poisoned, or too coarse.
paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all repair the same weak point: useful knowledge is scattered across linked evidence, and the system must decide which links deserve trust. RPO-RAG, GCA-KBQA, S-Path-RAG, HyperRAG, and the unified graph answer systems use relation paths to make question answering more grounded than free-form text generation. AID uses hypothesis subgraphs for conversational recommendation, asking clarifying questions only while several interpretations remain plausible. Knowledge-aware recommendation papers such as SEDIRec, the graph editing model, and spectral heterogeneous diffusion try to clean or enrich item and user evidence before ranking products. LOPE, document-to-graph work, and CompTox ontology construction focus on building consistent maps from scientific, web, or environmental information. DSTAG, continual knowledge graph learning, MetriKG, and dynamic crawling treat knowledge as changing over time rather than fixed. KEPo and poisoning work expose the hostile version of the same design: if attackers can alter graph evolution paths, linked evidence can make a language model confidently wrong. CausalSKyHop, causal knowledge graph papers, and fact-checking work use graphs to show which connected pieces explain, depend on, verify, or constrain others.
what_changed: The 2026 version of this family looks less like storing clean triples and more like running knowledge graphs inside messy systems. The evidence shows graphs tied to small language models, answer generation, fact checking, recommendation, finance fraud, table search, web crawling, 3D scene reasoning, biomedical edge classification, environmental monitoring, and multimodal reasoning. Language models appear as builders, users, and checkers of graphs, but the papers repeatedly add structure around them so fluent text does not replace verification. Another change is trust pressure: calibration, poisoning attacks, safe medical question answering, consistent extraction, dynamic updates, and profiling all treat graph quality as part of the task. Scale also matters, with fast rule mining, synthetic graph generation, and efficient path selection appearing as practical needs.
limits: These explanations rest on the input metadata and current repo JSON, not full paper bodies or independent results. The family assumes that graph links carry meaningful evidence, relation labels are reliable enough, and missing data is not hiding the crucial path. Those assumptions can fail in sparse user graphs, noisy scientific extraction, changing web data, or adversarial GraphRAG settings. Multimodal methods need text, image, and structure to describe compatible facts; otherwise fusion can join signals that should stay separate. Confidence and causal claims depend on whether the graph actually contains the needed alternatives and dependencies. Speedups and synthetic graphs may preserve common structure while losing rare facts. The evidence describes claimed problems and contributions, but does not prove deployment reliability across domains, languages, graph sizes, or attackers.
